title: Check and fix a found wood stove
summary: Go over a salvaged wood stove before it heats a room: the door seal, the glass, the firebrick, the baffle, the catalyst and the body. A stove that leaks or runs without its baffle overheats and spills smoke and carbon monoxide; an old one may have asbestos in its gasket.

materials.item: Fibreglass rope door gasket, same diameter and density as the old one
High-temperature silicone or stove gasket cement
Ceramic stove glass of the same size and spec as the old
Firebrick of the same type and size as the old
Spray bottle of water with a few drops of dish soap
P100 (P3) half-mask respirator, disposable gloves and a plastic sheet, for an old stove
CO alarm and smoke alarm for the stove room

steps.text: Find the certification label on the back. Write down the model, the clearances and the pipe size: the label overrides any manual (Drolet Part 1). No label means an uncertified stove, which needs much bigger clearances (NRCan wood heating).
Work on a cold stove. Shovel the ash into a metal can with a lid and set it outside, at least 3 m (10 ft) from buildings (Georgian Bay ashes).
steps.warn: Ashes can take several days to cool completely (Georgian Bay ashes). Live embers in ash give off carbon monoxide: never store ashes indoors, in a non-metal container or on a wooden deck (Drolet Part 1).

steps.text: If the stove is old, treat the door gasket and any grey board under or behind it as asbestos until proven otherwise. Mist it with soapy water, wear a P100 respirator and gloves, lay plastic underneath and keep others out (CPSC asbestos; for the respirator see the asbestos guide).
steps.warn: Don't brush, sweep or vacuum the dust. CPSC says not to scrape or break asbestos and to seal waste in plastic bags: keep it misted, pull the gasket out wet in as few pieces as you can and seal it in a plastic bag.

steps.text: Close and latch the door on a strip of paper or a bank note and pull. Repeat all the way round the door. If it slides out easily anywhere, the seal leaks (Drolet Escape 1800, EPA catalytic).
If the stove has a latch or hinge adjustment, tighten the door first and test again (Cornell maintenance, NRCan wood heating).

To replace the rope: take the old gasket out and scrape the old glue out of the groove with a screwdriver (keep it misted and the respirator on if step 3 applied). Lay a bead of high-temperature silicone about 5 mm (3/16 in) in the groove and press the new rope in, starting mid-way along the hinge side (Drolet Escape 1800).
steps.warn: Don't stretch the rope as you press it in, or it thins and leaks.

steps.text: Cut the rope about 13 mm (½ in) longer than the groove, push the end into the groove, tuck in loose fibres, close the door and leave it 24 hours before a fire (Drolet Escape 1800). Then do the paper test again.

Look at the door glass. Cracked or broken glass is replaced only with ceramic stove glass (Drolet Escape 1800). Centre it on its gasket and snug the retainer screws without over-tightening (Drolet Escape 1800).
steps.warn: Window glass and tempered glass are not ceramic stove glass. Drolet says not to use the stove if the glass is broken (Drolet Part 1).

steps.text: Lift out the baffle and air tubes and check for cracks, sagging tubes and loose parts (Cornell maintenance, NRCan wood heating). If the baffle has fibre board or blanket, wear gloves and a respirator: handle it like asbestos (Cornell maintenance).
steps.warn: Never run the stove with a cracked or missing baffle: it overheats (Drolet Part 1).

steps.text: Check the firebrick. Replace bricks that crumble, have cracks wider than 3 mm or deeper than 6 mm, or have worn away a quarter of their thickness, using the same type and size. The crack limits are Skamol's for its own stoves: follow your maker's if it gives others (Skamol policy, Cornell maintenance).
Catalytic stove: with the stove cold, shine a flashlight through the combustor and look for crumbling, peeling, missing pieces, clogging and gaps at its gasket (EPA catalytic).
Look over the body: welds, cast-iron panels and seams, legs and the flue collar. A cracked or badly warped welded steel body can't be repaired; strip it for parts (Cornell maintenance).
Put it back together and install it on a proper chimney before any fire (see the stove install guide). Fit a CO alarm and a smoke alarm in the room (Drolet Part 1).
First fires: open doors and windows, burn two or three small fires, then work up to hotter ones as the paint cures (Drolet Part 1). Watch every seam and the door for smoke.
steps.warn: If any part of the stove or pipe glows red, it is overfiring: close the air controls until it cools (DuraVent DTC).

notes:
## What you've found
The certification label on the back gives the model, the safety standard, the clearances and the pipe size, and it overrides the manual and anything else written about the stove (Drolet Part 1). A modern Canadian stove lists ULC S627 for safety and EPA or CSA B415.1 for emissions (Drolet Escape 1800).

No label means an uncertified stove: used and antique stoves, most built before the early 1980s, and stoves from small welding shops. They burn more wood and make more smoke and creosote, and they need far bigger clearances: 1,200 mm (48 in) from combustibles at the sides and back and 1,500 mm (60 in) above (NRCan wood heating). Stoves made before about 1991 could be turned down so far that they smouldered and built up creosote (Cornell maintenance). An uncertified stove can still keep you alive; give it the full clearances in [Install a salvaged wood stove](#guides/build_stove_install).

## Old stoves and asbestos
Door gaskets in wood and coal stoves may contain asbestos, and worn ones shed fibres in use. Walls and floors round old stoves may be covered with asbestos paper, millboard or cement sheet (CPSC asbestos). Treat it as asbestos, see [Spot likely asbestos](#guides/safety_asbestos_check) and the [asbestos hazard card](#browse/hazards/asbestos).

CPSC advises a professional for repair or removal and says not to saw, sand, scrape or drill asbestos. With none to hand, its steps for taking a sample are the closest guide: mist the material with water and a few drops of detergent, wear disposable gloves, lay plastic underneath, keep others out of the room, and never dust, sweep or vacuum the debris (CPSC asbestos). The asbestos guide covers the respirator: a paper dust mask doesn't stop the fibres. Material in good condition is best left alone (CPSC asbestos), so leave old millboard and cement sheet in place and don't break it; if it's crumbling, take the stove, not the board.

## The door gasket
**Test.** On a cold stove, close and latch the door on a strip of paper or a bank note and pull gently. Do it all the way round the door, because a gasket can seal on one side and leak on another (Drolet Escape 1800, EPA catalytic, Cornell maintenance). A haze of soot on one part of the glass also shows where a door leaks (NRCan wood heating).

**Adjust first.** Many stoves have latch or hinge adjustments to keep the door pressed on the gasket (NRCan wood heating). On a Drolet Escape 1800, pull the latch's split pin, give the handle one turn anticlockwise, and refit the pin (Drolet Escape 1800).

**Replace.** Use rope of the same diameter and density (Drolet Escape 1800). Door ropes run from about 10 to 25 mm (⅜ to 1 in) (Cornell maintenance); the Drolet Escape 1800 takes 16 mm (⅝ in). Kits come with cement or high-temperature silicone (Cornell maintenance). Drolet's method: scrape the groove clean, run a 5 mm (3/16 in) bead of high-temperature silicone, press the rope in from the middle of the hinge side without stretching it, cut it about 13 mm (½ in) longer than the groove, tuck the end and loose fibres in, close the door and wait 24 hours (Drolet Escape 1800). Other cements cure differently: follow the tube.

Some gaskets need replacing yearly, others last several years; check them at least once a year and now and then in the season (NRCan wood heating). Check the ash-pan door and any bypass damper gasket the same way (EPA catalytic).

## Door glass
Stove glass is a clear ceramic, not glass. Heat rarely breaks it; knocks do (NRCan wood heating). Drolet's glass is 4 mm (5/32 in) ceramic tested to 760 °C (1,400 °F), and a replacement must be ceramic of the same spec; most breaks come from the glass sitting off-centre or the retainer screws being over-tightened (Drolet Escape 1800). The label says to replace it with ceramic only, and Drolet says not to use the stove with broken glass (Drolet Escape 1800, Drolet Part 1). Window glass and tempered glass are not ceramic.

No maker approves a substitute: Drolet says never to use substitute materials and not to use the stove with broken glass (Drolet Escape 1800, Drolet Part 1). The only report of a stopgap is an owners' forum thread from 2011, where one poster had cut a sheet of 22-gauge plain steel to clamp over the door opening so the door gasket still seals, and another suggested bending sheet metal over the opening (Hearth.com glass thread). That is anecdote, not a tested repair: use it only if the alternative is no heat, and fit ceramic glass as soon as you can. Never galvanised steel, whose coating gives off dangerous gas when hot (NRCan wood heating), and never plywood, which Drolet lists as a material not to burn (Drolet Part 1).

The glass sits in a flat, self-adhesive woven fibreglass gasket, centred on the edge and folded round it without stretching (Drolet Escape 1800). Brown streaks coming in from the edge of the glass mean that gasket leaks (Drolet Part 1, Cornell maintenance). Clean the glass only when cold, and never with abrasives (Drolet Part 1).

## Firebrick
Hairline cracks are normal and the stove stays safe. Replace a brick when a crack is wider than 3 mm or deeper than 6 mm, when it has worn away more than a quarter of its thickness, or when it crumbles; the back bricks wear first because logs hit them (Skamol policy, written for its Chesneys stoves which have metal behind the bricks; EPA catalytic for crumbling or missing pieces). Use the same type and size as the original (Cornell maintenance). A Drolet Escape 1800 takes 21 bricks in three widths, all 9 in long and 1¼ in thick (Drolet Escape 1800). Grey bricks are cement and pumice; yellow ones are mostly silica (Drolet Part 1).

## Baffle and air tubes
The baffle sits at the top of the firebox and lasts anywhere from two to ten years. Air tubes and channels can come loose or fall into the firebox; put them back at once (NRCan wood heating). Stainless tubes sag or burn through with heat (Cornell maintenance). Running with a cracked or missing baffle causes unsafe temperatures (Drolet Part 1). A fibre blanket on top of the baffle must lie flat so it doesn't block the flue; handle the fibre like asbestos (Cornell maintenance), since ceramic fibre is a possible carcinogen (CAREX Canada RCF). Taking the baffle out also opens the way to sweep the chimney (Drolet Part 1); see [chimney sweeping](#guides/skill_chimney_sweeping).

## Catalytic combustor
A catalytic stove has a ceramic honeycomb and a bypass damper. The catalyst starts burning smoke at 177 to 316 °C (350 to 600 °F) and can be damaged by prolonged heat, so avoid temperatures near or above 870 °C (1,600 °F) (EPA catalytic).
- **Look:** with the stove cold, shine a light through it. Blocked cells mean creosote; check for crumbling, peeling, missing pieces and gaps at its gasket. Brush it with a soft brush; don't drop it, scrape it, blow it with high-pressure air or wet it hot (EPA catalytic).
- **Watch the chimney:** with a good fire going, open the bypass and look at the chimney top; close the bypass, wait 10 minutes and look again. Still smoking: check the combustor. Cracks in the honeycomb may not matter; missing pieces do (NRCan wood heating).
- **Life:** makers guarantee up to six years, but heavy use can finish one in one or two (NRCan wood heating).
- **Poison:** coal, kerosene, lighter fluid and other fuels not on the label can poison it; trash, treated wood and plywood make fly ash and harmful smoke (EPA catalytic). See [what to burn](#guides/reference_what_to_burn).

A dead catalyst stops cleaning up the smoke, so expect more creosote and check the chimney often (EPA catalytic).

## Cracks and warping
A cracked or badly distorted welded steel body can't be fixed. Warped inner steel parts are replaced. Cast iron usually cracks from overfiring, most often because of leaking joints (Cornell maintenance). Check cast-iron seams yearly and re-cement them as needed (EPA catalytic). Drolet warns that using a stove with cracked or broken glass, firebrick or baffle may be unsafe (Drolet Part 1); hairline firebrick cracks are the exception.

## First fires
Connect the stove to a sound chimney first: [Install a salvaged wood stove](#guides/build_stove_install), and [check the chimney](#guides/test_chimney). The first fires cure the paint: the fumes smell bad but aren't poisonous, and they can set off smoke alarms. Open doors and windows, burn two or three small fires, then hotter ones until the smell stops (Drolet Part 1). Small first fires also season the bricks (Skamol policy). Never start a fire with gasoline, naphtha, kerosene or lighter fluid (Drolet Part 1). A CO alarm and a smoke alarm belong in the stove's room (Drolet Part 1); see [carbon monoxide](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide). Glowing red metal means overfiring: close the air (DuraVent DTC).

## When to strip it for parts instead
- A cracked or warped welded body (Cornell maintenance).
- No baffle and no way to replace it.
- Broken glass with no ceramic replacement, unless you accept the unapproved steel-plate stopgap above.
The firebrick, ceramic glass, blower and plate steel are all worth taking.
